stories.title: The Maple and the Flame
passages: Marisol Fenn unlocked the workshop before dawn, the way she had every morning since Henrik died, and found a second notice from the landlord slid under the door, the red stamp bleeding through the thin paper. She did not open it. She already knew what it said, because the first one had said the same thing in gentler ink. On the workbench sat the Delacroix commission, returned two days earlier by a client who said the upper register sounded thin, though Marisol suspected he had simply changed his mind about the price. She ran her thumb along the f-hole, checking for a crack that was not there, and set it back in its case. The wood bin in the corner held barely enough spruce for one more top plate. She would have to ask Ostrander for credit again, and he had already told her twice that Henrik's name only carried a shop so far without Henrik in it. Outside, the El train rattled past, and she counted, out of habit, how many weeks of rent that sound represented. Not enough. She put on the kettle anyway and told herself the day would turn, because someone had to.

By Thursday the landlord stopped sliding notices under the door and came himself, standing in the doorway with his arms crossed while Marisol tried to explain that money from an upcoming competition might come through by spring. He gave her thirty days, not unkindly, and said Henrik would have understood a business decision better than sentiment. After he left, she called Ostrander about the spruce and found him even shorter with her than the landlord had been; he wanted the last invoice paid before he would cut another board, and he was not wrong to ask. She sat for a long while at Henrik's old bench, the one with his initials worn into the wood, and did the arithmetic again, the way she had done it every night that month, and it came out the same losing number every time. Her one apprentice, Dana, had already found part-time work at a bar to cover the gap in her stipend and apologized for it as though it were a betrayal. Marisol told her it was not. She looked at the half-finished violin under the window, the one she had started for herself, for no client at all, and wondered if she would have to sell it for parts before it ever sang.

A postcard-sized flyer for the Verrier Prize had been pinned to the workshop's corkboard for two months before Marisol actually read it closely, the deadline circled in Henrik's handwriting from before he died, as though he had meant to enter and never gotten around to it. The competition wanted a finished instrument, judged blind, by a panel that included makers she had only ever read about. She did not know if the violin under the window was good enough, or even finished enough; it needed another two weeks of varnish work she was not sure she had the material for. Dana thought she should try. Ostrander, when she mentioned it, shrugged and said entering cost nothing but the shipping, which was true and also not the point. Marisol spent an evening turning the instrument over in the lamplight, checking the arching against Henrik's old templates, unable to decide if she was looking at his best lesson or her own mistake wearing his shape. She filled out the entry form twice and did not send it either time. On the third night she walked it to the post office herself before she could change her mind again, and came home unsure whether she had done something hopeful or something foolish.

The acceptance letter came on a Tuesday, and Marisol read it standing in the doorway with her coat still on, twice, to be sure. The violin had made the semifinal round in Brussels, one of thirty instruments chosen from over four hundred entries. Dana whooped loud enough that a customer out front asked what had happened. There was still no money to speak of, but Marisol found she could breathe differently walking through the shop that afternoon, noticing things she had stopped noticing: the good light through the west window, the smell of the new varnish batch, the fact that Henrik's templates still hung exactly where he had left them. She called Ostrander mostly to tell someone, and he surprised her by offering to front the spruce for a small commission a friend of his wanted, no rush on payment. It was not rescue, not yet, but it was room to work. She spent the weekend packing the violin herself, wrapping it the way Henrik had taught her, layer by careful layer, and booked the cheapest flight to Brussels she could find, leaving eleven days before the competition, telling herself she would rather be there early and nervous than rushed and sorry.

In the recital hall in Brussels, a violinist named Colette Aubert lifted Marisol's violin without introduction and simply played, and the sound that came off the maple back filled the room in a way that made the row of judges stop writing. Marisol stood at the rear with her hand over her mouth. She had not expected to cry, and she had not expected the stranger two seats down, a luthier named Daniel Osei who had shown at the last three Verrier competitions, to lean over afterward and tell her, quietly, that he had recognized Henrik's arching before he had even seen her name on the program. He had trained under a maker who had trained under Henrik decades earlier; the lineage ran that deep. They talked for an hour in the hallway about wood and varnish and the strange, small world of people who built instruments by hand, and for the first time in two years Marisol felt like she belonged to something larger than the rent she owed. When Aubert found her afterward and asked to keep playing the violin through the final round, Marisol said yes before she had finished the sentence, giddy in a way she had not let herself be since Henrik's funeral.

The semifinal results were posted on a corkboard in the hotel lobby, the old-fashioned way, and Marisol found her own name near the top of a very short list before Daniel found it for her, laughing, and lifted her half off the ground in a hug that startled them both. She was through to the final four, the only American maker left in the competition, and the committee had scheduled Aubert to perform her violin again in the closing concert, this time before an audience instead of a panel. That evening Daniel took her to a small restaurant near the conservatory that he swore Henrik himself used to favor on his own trips through Brussels years before, and over a bottle of wine neither of them could quite afford, they traded stories about a man who had apparently left half of Europe's luthiers with the same stubborn habits. Marisol called Dana from the sidewalk afterward, both of them talking over each other with excitement, and then she called Ostrander, who said, gruffly, that he supposed he would cut the spruce either way. Walking back to the hotel past midnight, the city lit gold along the canal, she let herself believe, just for that night, that it was all going to work out.

When the final adjudicator read Marisol's name aloud as the winner of the Verrier Prize, the hall went strange and distant for a moment before the applause reached her, and Daniel had to steer her by the elbow up to the stage because her legs were not entirely cooperating. Aubert embraced her afterward and, in front of the assembled judges, asked formally if the violin might travel with her on the autumn concert tour across four countries, an honor the emcee said had only been extended twice before in the prize's history. Marisol thought of Henrik's initials worn into the workbench at home and had to look at the ceiling for a moment to keep from crying in front of the cameras. There was a check, more money than the shop had seen in two years combined, and a wall of photographers, and Daniel grinning at her from the wings like he had known all along. She called Dana at three in the morning Brussels time and neither of them cared about the hour. Later, alone in her hotel room, she set the empty violin case on the bed and simply sat with it, hardly able to believe the shape her life had taken in the span of nine days.

Back in Chicago, the shop phone rang more in a week than it had in the previous six months, and Marisol hired Dana on full-time before the girl could even ask, backdating her raise to the day of the Brussels announcement out of something like gratitude. A local paper ran a short profile with a photograph of her at Henrik's old bench, and three separate string quartets called about commissions, cautious at first and then less so once she quoted her new prices. Ostrander delivered a full order of spruce and maple without being asked twice, and joked that he had always known the shop would come good, which was not remotely true but Marisol let him have it. She spent her evenings catching up on repairs she had let slide for months, glad simply to have her hands full of ordinary, unglamorous work again. The landlord sent a friendly note this time, no red stamp, asking whether she would consider a longer lease. Aubert's people were finalizing tour dates for the autumn, and Marisol had started, cautiously, to imagine what the shop might look like with two benches instead of one, Henrik's legacy widening instead of just barely surviving under her hands.

A quartet that had promised a deposit for two matched violins went quiet for a week and then wrote back to say they were reconsidering the budget, which left Marisol with wood already cut and no clear buyer for it. Around the same time, Aubert's manager emailed to say the autumn tour dates were being reshuffled by the presenting orchestras and that confirmation might slip by a month or two, nothing to worry about, just logistics. Marisol told Dana both things in the same breath and neither of them was sure how to feel about either one. Ostrander, when she mentioned the quartet, said that was just how commissions went sometimes, easy come, easy go, and he was not wrong, but it needled at her more than she let on. She spent an afternoon reorganizing the shop's books, trying to see the numbers clearly, and they told her nothing dramatic either way: not the freefall of two years ago, not the momentum of Brussels, just a shop treading its own water while it waited to hear back from people who owed it answers. She left work that evening unsure whether the quiet week meant something or nothing at all.

The email from Aubert's manager, when it finally came, said the autumn tour had lost its lead sponsor and would not go forward in its planned form, and that the violin's place in any future program was, for now, unresolved. On its heels came a message from an acquaintance forwarding a link to a small trade blog, where a maker Marisol had never met suggested, in passive and lawyerly language, that the Verrier judging panel had shown favoritism toward makers with 'documented lineage,' an unmistakable jab at Henrik's name attached to her own. It gained enough traction that two of her newer clients asked, awkwardly, whether the prize had been fully above board. Marisol answered every message she could and stopped answering the ones that were not really questions. The quartet's cut wood still sat unclaimed in the corner. Dana kept the shop running through it, quieter than usual, while Marisol spent long hours at Henrik's bench doing repair work that paid the bills but felt, for the first time since Brussels, like retreat rather than choice. She told herself it would blow over. She was no longer sure she believed it.

The fire started sometime after two in the morning, an electrician determined weeks later, in wiring behind the old finishing room that no one had thought to replace since Henrik's time. By the time the alarm reached Marisol's phone and she got a cab to the block, the street was already blocked by two engines, and there was nothing to do but stand behind the tape in her coat over pajamas and watch the windows glow orange and then black. Dana arrived crying before Marisol had said a word to her. Everything in the back room was gone by morning: the wood stock, the templates worn to the shape of Henrik's hands, the half-built commissions, the tools she had used every day for six years. The violin that had won in Brussels was safe, still in Europe with Aubert's people, and for one disoriented moment that felt like the only mercy in the whole ruin, before the scale of everything else caught up with her. She sat on the curb as the sun came up, soot on her sleeves, and could not, for a long time, make herself walk into what was left of the building to see it in the light.

The insurance adjuster's report took three weeks and answered almost nothing that mattered to Marisol, who stood in the gutted workshop most days regardless, unable to stay away and unable to be useful there either. Henrik's workbench had burned down to a blackened frame, the initials gone with the rest of it, and she found herself grieving that detail more sharply than the lost inventory, though the inventory was gone too, all of it, eleven years of accumulated wood and half a life of tools. Dana had gone back to the bar full-time and cried on the phone when she said so, apologizing again for something that still was not her fault. Ostrander came by once, looked at the ash where his spruce had been stacked, and did not offer to cut anything this time; there was nothing left to build. Aubert sent a kind, useless message from a tour stop in Lisbon. Marisol answered it two days late, out of a hollowness she did not have words for yet, and then sat alone in the burned room as the light went from the empty window frame, unable to imagine what Monday, or the one after it, was supposed to look like now.

stories.title: A Fair Wind Home
passages: At the Whampoa anchorage, Silas Bramwell watched the carpenters work by lamplight on a sprung plank near the Kestrel's bow, the third such repair since they had limped in from a typhoon three weeks before, and did sums in his head that never once came out in his favor. His father had died owing more than the firm's warehouse was worth, and the letter Silas carried folded in his coat, four months old by the time it reached him, said the creditors had agreed to wait only until the next tea fleet came home. The Kestrel was the only ship Bramwell and Sons had left, and she was, at that moment, more patched than sound. His purser found him that morning to say two hands had taken their pay and gone ashore for good, unwilling to sail again under a captain whose owners might not exist by the time they returned. Silas paid the carpenters from his own pocket, the last of it, and stood at the rail afterward watching junks move across the brown water, trying to remember what it had felt like, as a boy, to think his father's name meant something steady.

Three days later the tea merchant Silas had contracted with, a cautious man named Ho Chen, sent word that he could not extend credit on the season's first-picked leaf without half payment in advance, silver Silas did not have, not since the carpenters. Rumor along the anchorage said Captain Reeve of the Osprey had already paid Ho Chen's price outright and secured the finest chests for himself, which would put Reeve's ship a full week ahead before either of them cleared the river. Silas sent word to his brother Robbie, serving as second mate aboard the Kestrel, and found him already at the merchant's door trying, badly, to negotiate in his poor Cantonese. Between the two of them they scraped together enough by pawning what plate and instruments they had brought from home, including their late father's sextant, to secure a lesser but still respectable parcel of leaf. It felt, walking back to the ship in the rain, less like a plan than a postponement of ruin. Silas did not tell Robbie about the creditors' deadline. He told himself it was mercy, though it felt, even to him, more like cowardice wearing mercy's coat.

They cleared the Bogue on the morning tide, the Kestrel low and heavy with her hold full of chests, and for the first time in a month Silas had nothing left to negotiate, borrow, or repair, only the sea in front of him and the Osprey's topsails already small on the horizon ahead. The crew, short-handed but rested, went about the ordinary business of a ship finding her trim, and Robbie kept the noon sightings with their father's sextant, freshly redeemed, as though nothing had happened to it at all. Silas walked the deck twice a day checking the mended plank, which held, and said little to anyone. There was no way yet to know whether the season would save the firm or finish it; the voyage was three months of sea in either direction, and a hundred things, weather and reefs and fever and the Osprey's head start, could decide it before London ever came into view. He wrote a short letter to Eleanor Gale that he intended to send back with the pilot boat, telling her only that they were underway, and found he could not, honestly, tell her more than that, because he did not yet know more than that himself.

A fortnight out, a steady quartering wind took hold of the Kestrel and did not let go, and Silas watched his log entries fill with numbers he had not dared hope for at Whampoa. On the ninth day of the fair run they raised a sail on the horizon that Robbie, aloft with the glass, identified after a long minute as the Osprey herself, and by dusk they had drawn close enough to exchange signals, a courtesy between rival captains that masked, poorly, how much each wanted to know of the other's progress. The Kestrel's new canvas, bought against Silas's better judgment back in London, was earning its cost twice over in speed. The crew felt it too; there was less grumbling at the capstan and more wagering over which cape they would raise first. Silas allowed himself, cautiously, to write actual figures into the margin of his log: if the wind held even half as well past the Cape, they might make London inside four months, which would be a fast season by any measure and, more importantly, a season fast enough. He did not say the word lucky aloud, from old habit, but he thought it.

They took the Cape in weather that should by rights have cost them a week and instead cost them two days, running before a gale that Silas, watching the following seas lift the Kestrel's stern like a hand, judged the finest piece of sailing he had seen in fifteen years at sea. The old hands said as much afterward, which from that crew amounted to a kind of ovation. Robbie came below soaked through and grinning, reporting that the Osprey had fallen astern in the same blow and had not been sighted since noon. That night Silas allowed a double ration of grog and sat late with Robbie over the chart, the two of them working the reckoning together the way they had not since they were boys racing skiffs on the home river, their father shouting encouragement from the bank. For the first time since their father's funeral, Silas let himself talk about what the firm might look like once the debts were cleared, a second ship, perhaps, with Robbie for her master. Robbie laughed at the size of the ambition and then admitted, quietly, that he wanted exactly that. Above them the rigging sang in a wind that felt, finally, like it was blowing them toward something rather than away from ruin.

By the time the Kestrel raised the Lizard, Silas had not slept properly in two days and did not care in the least. They had outrun the Osprey by nearly four hundred miles in the final leg, a lead confirmed when a homeward pilot boat came alongside with newspapers and the cheerful, disbelieving news that no other tea ship had yet been sighted in the Channel that season. The pilot also carried a letter from Eleanor, written on the chance it might reach him, saying simply that she would be watching from the Pool of London for the first ship's colors, whichever they turned out to be. Robbie read it over Silas's shoulder without asking and then clapped him hard enough on the back to stagger him. Silas ordered fresh paint slapped over the Kestrel's scarred bow that same afternoon, unwilling to come up the river looking as patched as she had left Whampoa. The crew, sensing the end of a long chase, worked with an energy he had not seen from them since Canton. Silas stood at the rail that evening watching the English coast thicken from a smudge into hills and fields, and let himself believe, finally and without caution, that they were going to win.

The Kestrel came up the Thames on the morning tide with her signal flags reading first ship, new season's tea, and the crowd that had gathered along the wharves, alerted by runners since dawn, gave a cheer that Silas felt in his chest before he properly heard it. Ho Chen's leaf, sold that same afternoon at the premium reserved for the season's first cargo home, brought a price that cleared every debt his father had left and put a sum besides into the firm's account that Silas had to have read back to him twice to believe. Eleanor was waiting exactly where her letter had promised, and Robbie, grinning, made himself scarce the moment he saw her, leaving Silas to cross the wharf alone. The Osprey came in two days later to a much quieter reception, which Silas, generous in victory, did not mention to Reeve when they shook hands that evening at the exchange. There was a dinner in the Kestrel's honor, and a toast to their father that left Silas unable to speak for a moment, and underneath the noise and the gladness a single steady thought he kept returning to all night: the firm, against every arithmetic of the spring, was saved.

In the weeks after the Kestrel's homecoming, Silas found himself busier than the voyage had ever made him, meeting brokers who wanted first refusal on the firm's next cargo and a shipwright who quoted him, almost apologetically, a fair price for a proper refit of the bow. He paid off the last of his father's creditors in person, one by one, taking a plain satisfaction in watching each man mark the ledger closed. Robbie had taken to walking the wharves with a proprietary air that made Silas laugh, already talking as though the second ship they had dreamed of off the Cape were merely a matter of paperwork. Eleanor's father, who had discouraged the match a year earlier on the perfectly reasonable grounds of the firm's debts, now asked Silas to dinner with a warmth that Silas accepted without comment on the timing. The Kestrel herself sat in dry dock getting new copper on her hull, and Silas visited most mornings to watch the work, still faintly disbelieving that the battered ship that had left Whampoa patched and borrowed-against was the same one being fitted now for a season she had more than earned.

A customs clerk flagged an irregularity in the Kestrel's manifest, a discrepancy between the weight declared at Whampoa and the weight landed, small enough to be a clerical error and large enough that it required a formal inquiry before the bond could be released. Silas was not overly troubled; such things happened often enough with cargo that had crossed a typhoon season, and his broker assured him it was routine. Still, it meant a portion of the season's profit sat frozen in bond rather than in the firm's account, and the shipwright's refit, half-finished, could not be paid out in full until the inquiry closed. Robbie thought it was nothing. Eleanor's father asked about it once, carefully, in a way that made Silas suspect the man's warmth had conditions attached after all. Silas spent two mornings at the customs house answering questions about stowage and ballast that felt, to him, entirely beside the point, and came away each time no more informed than when he had arrived. It was neither the triumph of the homecoming nor any kind of disaster, just a stalled ledger and a question mark hanging over money he had already, in his mind, spent twice over.

The inquiry's finding, when it finally came, was worse than Silas had let himself expect: a portion of the tea, stowed nearest the sprung plank they had patched at Whampoa, had taken on damp during the Cape crossing and been quietly dried and remixed with sound leaf before landing, a decision made by the mate at Whampoa without Silas's knowledge, but made in his ship all the same. The bond authority released only a partial sum and referred the matter to the brokers' guild, whose censure, though it carried no fine, was printed in the shipping notices for every rival and creditor in London to read. Two of the new contracts he had been courting quietly withdrew. The shipwright, unpaid in full, put a lien on the refit and stopped the work with the Kestrel's hull half-coppered and unfit for sea. Eleanor's father did not raise the subject of dinner again. Robbie blamed himself for the mate's decision, made under his nominal watch, and grew quiet in a way Silas had not seen in him since their father's death. Silas spent a bad week trying to explain to men who no longer entirely believed him that the firm was still, in fact, sound.

To save the cost of the shipwright's yard, Silas decided to move the half-coppered Kestrel downriver himself on the evening tide to a cheaper mooring, a short run he had made a hundred times and saw no reason to hire a river pilot for. The gale came up faster than the glass had promised, catching the ship still in the narrows with her new copper only half-fastened along one side and her handling, as a result, badly uneven. She struck a mooring chain in the dark and swung broadside before Silas could bring her off, driving hard onto the mud below Blackwall with a shudder that threw two men from the rigging. Robbie, out on the bowsprit trying to secure a parted line, was pitched into the black water as the bow dropped, and though they had a boat over the side within minutes, the tide and the cold had already taken him by the time they found him. Silas held his brother on the mud flat as the rest of the crew stood back, unable to make himself believe what his own hands were telling him. The Kestrel herself broke her back on the falling tide before morning, and by dawn there was nothing left of either of them, ship or brother, that could be saved.

They buried Robbie on a grey Thursday with half the wharves in attendance, men who had cheered the Kestrel's homecoming eleven weeks earlier now standing silent in the same coats. Eleanor stood beside Silas through the service and did not let go of his arm, though he registered her presence only distantly, the way he registered most things that week, as if from behind glass. The Kestrel's wreck was declared not worth salvaging, and what remained of the season's profit, already thinned by the guild's censure, went to settle the last of the firm's obligations before there was nothing left to call Bramwell and Sons at all. Ho Chen sent a formal letter of condolence that Silas could not bring himself to answer. He walked down to Blackwall once, alone, to look at the mud flat where the ribs of his ship still showed at low tide, black and half-buried, and stood there a long time without any thought he could afterward remember having. Their father's sextant, the one he and Robbie had pawned and redeemed together at Whampoa, had gone down with the ship. Silas went home that evening to a house that felt, for the first time in his life, entirely empty.
